conceptTag: Why airlines struggle to make money
readerTitle: Why airlines move the world and keep so little of the money
caseNote: 실제 기업 (USAir와 Berkshire Hathaway의 1989년 투자, 미국 항공업계) + 가상 적용 (화물 운송 회사 vs 배차 소프트웨어)
insight: 수익성은 회사의 실력보다 먼저 산업 구조가 정한다. 수요가 크게 늘어도 그 돈은 힘이 센 쪽으로 흘러간다.
misconception: 수요가 꾸준히 늘고 경영진이 유능하면 그 산업의 회사는 돈을 번다.

sources.text: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters: 1989 (USAir preferred stock purchase), 1994 (USAir write-down), 2007 (Kitty Hawk remark). berkshirehathaway.com/letters
Porter, M. (2008). The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
Chapter 11 filings of United (2002), US Airways (2002, 2004), Delta and Northwest (2005), American (2011), widely reported in news coverage
IATA industry economic performance reports (thin industry net margins over time)
Berkshire Hathaway 2020 annual meeting (sale of airline stocks)

factChecks.note: Berkshire가 1989년 USAir 우선주에 투자했고, 이후 USAir가 배당을 중단했으며 Berkshire가 1994년에 장부가를 크게 낮췄다는 내용은 1989년·1994년 주주서한으로 확인하세요. 투자 금액은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
Kitty Hawk 발언은 2007년 주주서한에 나오는 것으로 알려져 있습니다. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 풀어서 썼습니다. 게시 전에 연도와 표현을 원문과 대조하세요.
미국 대형 항공사들의 Chapter 11 신청 연도(United 2002, US Airways 2002·2004, Delta·Northwest 2005, American 2011)를 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "several of the largest US airlines"로만 적었습니다.
Berkshire가 2016년경 미국 대형 항공사 주식을 다시 샀다가 2020년 팬데믹 때 모두 팔았다는 내용은 2020년 주주총회 보도로 확인하세요.
"업계 전체가 장기간 번 돈이 적다"는 정성적 서술입니다. IATA 자료로 대략적인 경향만 확인하고, 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why airlines move the world and keep so little of the money
body: Air travel has grown for most of the past century. Billions of people now fly every year, and almost nobody wants to give it up.
Yet over that long history, the airline industry as a whole has kept remarkably little profit. Several of the biggest US airlines have gone bankrupt, some more than once.

image.label: A packed airport with a nearly empty piggy bank
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 승객으로 붐비는 공항 탑승구 앞에, 동전이 몇 개만 든 투명 돼지저금통이 놓여 있음. 비행기에는 실제 항공사 로고나 도장을 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 1989. An airline wants your money.
body: You're an investor famous for buying strong, durable businesses. A large US airline offers you a big stake on generous terms. Air travel is growing, and you like its managers.

options.text: Invest. Demand is growing and the team is good
options.feedback: Growth and good managers help. But if the industry hands most of its value to others, even a well-run airline can struggle to keep any.

options.text: First study who keeps the money in this industry, then decide
options.feedback: You may miss a quick win, but you avoid betting on a business whose profits are squeezed from every side. That's the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Invest, but only through safer shares that pay a fixed dividend
options.feedback: Better protection than plain shares. Still, that dividend only gets paid if the airline earns money, so the industry's problems become yours.

cards.title: Warren Buffett picked option C.
body: In 1989, Berkshire Hathaway bought preferred shares in USAir, a type of share that promises a fixed dividend. Within a few years, USAir stopped paying that dividend, and Berkshire **wrote down** the shares, meaning it cut their value on its books.
Buffett later called the purchase a mistake. In his 2007 letter, he joked that a farsighted investor at Kitty Hawk would have done everyone a favor by shooting down Orville Wright's first plane.

cards.title: Industry structure sets the average
body: Michael Porter's **five forces** describe who takes a share of an industry's money: buyers, suppliers, rivals, new entrants and substitutes.

When all five are strong, the average company keeps little, no matter how many customers it serves. Airlines are a classic case. Porter himself used them as an example of an industry where every force pushes against profit.

image.label: An airplane pulled at from five sides
image.brief: 가운데 비행기 한 대를 다섯 방향에서 밧줄로 끌어당기는 일러스트. 밧줄마다 "Buyers", "Suppliers", "Rivals", "New entrants", "Substitutes" 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Every force pushes the same way.
body: Put together, the airline is caught between price-shopping travelers on one side and powerful suppliers on the other.

breakdown.label: Buyers
breakdown.detail: Fare-search sites make price the main choice

breakdown.label: Suppliers
breakdown.detail: Few jet makers, volatile fuel, unions, crowded airports

breakdown.label: Rivalry
breakdown.detail: High fixed costs and seats worth nothing after takeoff

breakdown.label: New entrants
breakdown.detail: Leased planes make starting an airline possible

breakdown.label: Substitutes
breakdown.detail: Trains, cars and video calls on shorter trips

cards.title: Bad times don't clear the field.
body: In many industries, weak companies close and the survivors raise prices. Airlines often don't vanish. Under US bankruptcy law, an airline can keep flying while it cuts its debts and costs.
So the planes stay in the sky, the seats stay for sale, and fares stay low. Meanwhile, the money tends to flow to players with fewer rivals, such as aircraft makers and busy airports.
cards.softwareNote: Many app markets look like this: users compare prices in seconds, switching is free and new rivals launch cheaply. Heavy demand alone won't make those apps profitable.

cards.title: Structure sets the average, not your fate.
body: Some airlines, such as Southwest and Ryanair, stayed profitable for long stretches by building a very different, low-cost system.

Forces also shift. After a wave of mergers in the 2010s, US airlines had several good years, and Buffett bought airline shares again. When the pandemic hit in 2020, he sold them all. A bad structure can improve, but it can turn quickly too.

cards.title: Two businesses for sale.
body: Both sell to the same trucking market. One is a regional freight company: dozens of rivals, shippers who rebid every contract, fuel as a major cost. The other sells dispatch software to trucking firms, which takes months to set up and has three serious rivals.
Same price. Which do you buy?

options.text: The freight company. It has far more revenue
options.feedback: More revenue, but every force squeezes it, much like an airline. Revenue tells you little about what you get to keep.

options.text: The software, if customers really find it hard to switch
options.feedback: Few rivals and real switching costs let it keep more of each sale. Check that the lock-in is real before paying for it.
Growth matters, but airlines grew for decades. Look at who holds the power before you look at growth.

cards.softwareNote: The dispatch software plays the role that aircraft makers play for airlines: a supplier with few rivals, selling into a crowded industry.

cards.title: Big demand doesn't mean big profits.
body: Before judging a business, ask who holds the power around it. An industry can serve billions of customers and still leave its companies with very little.
**Try it today:** list your biggest customer, supplier and rival. For each, write who would win if you argued over price.
